notes: What each budget head is, and for the largest of them what it is actually spent on. A budget head is named for accountants — 'Capital Outlay on Defence Services' tells a taxpayer nothing, and a demand's own description says only that it is a demand. `summary` is one short line: what this body does, enough to tell it from its neighbours. It is uncited, because it describes a remit rather than asserting a figure. `spentOn` is the longer itemised account with published amounts, so it must be cited; amounts quoted are the Actual 2024-25 column of the cited Notes on Demands. House style is in CONTRIBUTING.md — describe the mechanism, never appraise it.

items.summary: PM-Kisan cash transfers, crop insurance under Fasal Bima, and the interest subsidy that makes crop loans cheap.
items.spentOn: Half of it is cash paid straight to farmers: ₹66,121 crore under PM-Kisan. Most of the rest lowers the cost of credit and insurance: ₹24,600 crore to agricultural lending institutions, ₹17,812 crore covering the interest banks forgo on concessional crop loans, and ₹14,473 crore towards crop insurance premiums.

cite.locator: Demand No. 1, PM-Kisan / Agricultural Financial Institutions / MISS / PM Fasal Bima Yojana, Actual 2024-25

items.summary: The ICAR network — agricultural universities, crop and animal science institutes, and farm research stations.
Nuclear power stations run by NPCIL, plus the atomic research establishments behind them.
The National AYUSH Mission and the ayurveda, yoga, unani, siddha and homoeopathy institutes — AIIA, the research councils.
The chemicals and petrochemicals industry: HIL India, the petrochemicals technology institutes, and plastics parks.
Urea and nutrient-based fertiliser subsidy, paid to manufacturers and importers so fertiliser sells below cost.
items.spentOn: Paid to fertiliser manufacturers and importers rather than to farmers directly: ₹1,03,320 crore to domestic urea producers, ₹21,000 crore to urea importers, and ₹52,810 crore for phosphatic and potassic fertilisers. The payment covers the gap between what the fertiliser costs to make or import and the controlled price farmers pay for it.

cite.locator: Demand No. 6, items 2.01, 2.04, 3.01 and 3.04 with their explanatory notes, Actual 2024-25

items.summary: Jan Aushadhi generic medicine stores, the NIPER pharmacy institutes, and pharmaceutical production incentives.
Airports Authority of India, the UDAN regional connectivity scheme, the DGCA, and Air India's residual debt.
Coal India and NLC India, plus mine safety and coal conservation work.
Export promotion: the interest equalisation scheme for exporters, duty drawback, and the tea, coffee, rubber and spices boards.
Startup Fund of Funds, industrial corridors, the patent and trademark offices, and GST refunds to industry.
India Post — the post office network, its staff and pensions, IT modernisation, and India Post Payments Bank.
Capital for BSNL and MTNL, telecom pensions, C-DOT research, and rural connectivity through the USO Fund.
items.spentOn: Mostly capital put into state-owned telecom companies: ₹72,514 crore to BSNL and ₹1,196 crore to MTNL. A further ₹18,500 crore goes to the Universal Service Obligation Fund, which pays operators to run networks in places they would not otherwise serve.

cite.locator: Demand No. 13, Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited / Mahanagar Telephone Nigam / Universal Service Obligation Fund, Actual 2024-25

items.summary: The Price Stabilisation Fund that buys and releases onions and pulses, consumer courts, and weights and measures.
Free foodgrain under PMGKAY, and the Food Corporation of India that buys, stores and moves the grain.
items.spentOn: Almost the whole demand — ₹1,99,500 crore of ₹2,07,706 crore — is PMGKAY, the free foodgrain scheme. The money is the gap between what the Food Corporation of India pays to buy and store grain and what it is then handed out for; ₹75,495 crore of it goes to the Corporation itself.

cite.locator: Demand No. 15, Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana and Food Corporation of India, Actual 2024-25

items.summary: Computerising village credit societies, cooperative training institutes, and the cooperative sugar and dairy sector.
Company registration and filings, the Competition Commission, the audit regulator NFRA, and the PM Internship Scheme.
The Archaeological Survey of India, national museums, the akademies for art and letters, and heritage conservation.
The Coast Guard, Border Roads Organisation, defence estates and the ministry's civilian secretariat — not the armed forces themselves.
Pay, rations, fuel, spares and maintenance for the Army, Navy and Air Force, and DRDO's running costs.
items.spentOn: Running the armed forces rather than equipping them: pay, rations, fuel, spares and maintenance. The Army takes ₹1,98,026 crore of it, the Air Force ₹49,332 crore and the Navy ₹32,735 crore. Buying aircraft, ships and vehicles is a separate demand, and so are pensions.

cite.locator: Demand No. 20, Defence Services - Army / Navy / Air Force / R&D, Actual 2024-25

items.summary: Aircraft and aero engines, warships, submarines, vehicles and ordnance — the capital half of the defence budget.
items.spentOn: Equipment, not people: ₹52,205 crore on other equipment, ₹44,365 crore on aircraft and aero engines, ₹25,567 crore on the naval fleet, ₹14,097 crore on research and development and ₹5,619 crore on naval dockyards. Salaries sit in Defence Services (Revenue) and pensions in Defence Pensions.

cite.locator: Demand No. 21, Aircraft and Aero Engines / Naval Fleet / Other Equipments / R&D, Actual 2024-25

items.summary: Pensions for retired armed forces personnel and their families, including the one-rank-one-pension revisions.
items.spentOn: Pensions and retirement benefits for former armed forces personnel and their families. At ₹1,57,654 crore this is almost exactly the size of the entire defence equipment budget — for every rupee spent on new aircraft, ships and vehicles, close to another rupee goes to those who have already served.

cite.locator: Demand No. 22, Pensions and other Retirement Benefits, Actual 2024-25

Forest and wildlife protection, Project Tiger and Project Elephant, pollution control boards, and climate change work.
Embassies and consulates, aid to Bhutan, Nepal, Afghanistan and Africa, and India's dues to the UN and its agencies.
The budget-making arm of the finance ministry, plus lines of credit to other countries and the SWAMIH stalled-housing fund.

Recapitalising public sector banks and insurers, the RuPay and BHIM incentive, and pension schemes like PM Vaya Vandana.
Oversight of state-owned companies and their performance monitoring.
Selling government stakes in public sector companies, and managing what is left of them.
Passes GST compensation to states, and runs the GST network, Enforcement Directorate and narcotics control.
items.spentOn: Despite the name, ₹1,44,007 crore of this — around 94% — is not tax administration at all but grants handed onward to state governments. Only what is left over runs the departments that collected the tax in the first place.

cite.locator: Demand No. 35, Grants-in-aid to State Governments, Actual 2024-25

items.summary: The income tax department — collecting income tax, corporation tax and securities transaction tax.
Customs and GST collection, plus export incentive payouts under RoDTEP and RoSCTL.
The CAG's audit staff, who check how every other line in this budget was actually spent.
Interest on money the government has already borrowed, including ₹34,162 crore owed to foreign lenders.
items.spentOn: Interest on money borrowed by previous governments, ₹34,162 crore of it owed to foreign lenders. It is the carrying cost of past borrowing rather than a purchase of anything this year; repaying the principal is a separate transaction elsewhere in the accounts. This is the single largest line in the budget, bigger than everything spent on defence.

cite.locator: Demand No. 39, Interest Payments and Interest on External Debt, Actual 2024-25

items.summary: Repaying the principal on money previously borrowed — distinct from Interest Payments, which is the cost of carrying it.
Pensions for retired central government civilian employees — not soldiers or railway staff, who have their own lines.
items.spentOn: Pensions and retirement benefits for retired central government civilian employees. Retired soldiers and railway staff are not in here — they are paid from separate lines, and defence pensions alone come to ₹1,57,654 crore, well over this.

cite.locator: Demand No. 41, Pensions and other Retirement Benefits, Actual 2024-25

items.summary: 50-year interest-free capital loans to states, Finance Commission grants, and disaster relief — on top of their tax share.
items.spentOn: Not the states' constitutional share of central taxes — that is deducted before the union spends anything and does not appear in this budget at all. This is what the union grants on top, and half of it is a conditional loan: ₹1,49,484 crore of 50-year interest-free lending that a state only draws by qualifying for it.

cite.locator: Demand No. 42, items 9 to 16 and Finance Commission Grants, Actual 2024-25

items.spentOn: The central armed police forces, not the state police you deal with day to day: CRPF ₹34,021 crore, BSF ₹27,939 crore, CISF ₹15,380 crore, ITBP ₹9,337 crore and Assam Rifles ₹7,977 crore. cite.locator: Demand No. 51, items 1.01 to 1.06 and Delhi Police, Actual 2024-25
